1.open: Think of a time someone gave you a warning you didn't want to hear. Who was it, and were you glad of it later?
questions: Jude introduces himself as "a servant of Jesus Christ" (v. 1), though by long tradition he was also Jesus's brother. What does it tell you that he chose that title first?

Jude says he planned to write about "the salvation we share" but felt he had to urge them to "contend earnestly for the faith" (v. 3). What is the difference between contending for the faith and just winning arguments?
Verse 4 says some people "turn the grace of our God into a license for immorality." How can grace be misused like that, and how do we tell it apart from real grace?
In verses 5 to 7 Jude points to people who had been rescued or privileged and still turned away. What do you make of the idea that a good start does not settle everything?
Jude says the troublemakers are "shepherding only themselves" (v. 12). What does healthy care for a community look like by comparison, in a church, a family or a small group?

Jude tells his readers to "keep yourselves in the love of God" (v. 21), and yet ends by praising the One "able to keep you from stumbling" (v. 24). Christians read how those fit together in different ways. How do you hear them together?

Jude says to "have mercy on those who doubt" (v. 22). If you have ever had doubts, what helped you most, or what would have helped? If doubt is not your struggle, how could you walk with someone who has it?
Verses 20 and 21 give simple practices: building up your faith, praying, and waiting for Christ's mercy. Which one feels most doable for you right now, and which feels hardest?
1.life: Pick one person who is struggling with faith or has drifted from it. This week, reach out with no agenda except kindness, and listen more than you talk.
1.prayer: Thank God that he is able to keep you from stumbling and present you with great joy. Ask for steady faith, and for a merciful heart toward people who doubt.
1.tip: The middle of the letter has harsh images and references to Jewish writings outside the Bible (vv. 9, 14-15). Don't get stuck there. Say briefly that Jude drew on traditions his readers knew, then steer the group back to the opening call and the closing verses, where the hope and the mercy are.
